newsitem.title: USA: Mich. district mulls move in bond counsel lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Mich. district mulls move in bond counsel lawsuit.

text.p: A Michigan school district has yet to make a decision on its next move in a lawsuit it brought against its bond counsel, the lawyer for the school district said Thursday.
Dennis Pollard said he plans to meet next week with Pontiac School District officials to determine whether to appeal a recent ruling by the Michigan Court of Appeals to the state supreme court.

The 3 to 0 state appeals court ruling that became public this week dismissed a conflict of interest claim against Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone and ruled that two remaining claims in the district's lawsuit should be retried.

Miller Canfield, Pontiac schools' bond counsel for a 1991 issue, was found liable of legal malpractice stemming from a conflict of interest claim in 1994 by a Oakland County Circuit Court jury, which awarded the district damages of $22 million to $28 million.
The judge presiding over the case subsequently set the award at $25.6 million plus interest -- the largest ever awarded in the county.

The Pontiac School District filed the lawsuit in connection with a 1991 $54.6 million bond issue, which included about $35 million of capital appreciation bonds. The district charged that Miller Canfield also represented Kemper Securities, Inc., the senior manager on the deal, without the district's consent.

The district also charged that Miller Canfield had omitted language in the ballot proposal for the bond issue that would have allowed the district, as it had intended, to use bond proceeds to buy land for a bus service and storage facility.
In addition, the lawsuit claimed the law firm misinterpreted to the district's detriment the Michigan State School Act of 1979 when the firm helped strucuture the bond issue.
Pollard said he was disappointed in the appeals' court ruling, adding that if the school district decides to appeal to the Michigan Supreme Court, all three claims would be part of that appeal.
Thomas Linn, a partner at Miller Canfield, said the firm's outside litigator did not believe the state's high court would take up an appeal.
Linn called the appeals court ruling "a terrific result" for the law firm, which had to post a $20 million bond during the appeals process.
He added that the ruling may restart settlement talks in the case.

The original verdict and award in the case sent shock waves through the bond counsel community nationwide. In 1994, the Michigan Legislature passed a law requiring school districts to obtain better disclosure from prospective bond counsels. Lawmakers also banned the use of capital appreciation bonds by school districts.
